card.title: Patterns of biodiversity — global and Nepal

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Biodiversity is richest toward the equator because of time, stability and energy. The number of species grows with area as S = c A^z, more slowly than area itself. Nepal's richness comes from a huge altitude range and from lying in the Himalaya and Indo-Burma hotspots, each of which must combine high endemism with heavy habitat loss.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
S = c A^z, where S is species number, A is area, c is a constant and z is the slope.
log S = log c + z log A.
Hotspot thresholds: endemic vascular plants >= 1500, and original habitat lost > 70 percent.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: A hotspot is not simply a place with many species. It also requires many endemics and severe habitat loss. A well-preserved forest with few unique species is not a hotspot.  ·  The species-area curve does not say that every extra hectare adds the same number of species. The rise flattens: the first hectares add many species, later hectares add fewer.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Quote z as a range, not a single number: about 0.1-0.2 locally, about 0.6-1.2 for very large areas.  ·  Do not call every protected forest a hotspot. Protected status and hotspot status are different ideas.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Amazon rainforest and Indo-Pacific coral reefs illustrate high equatorial richness.  ·  Chitwan's lowland forest and the Annapurna mid-hills hold different communities along Nepal's altitude gradient.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Equatorial richness is not caused only by heat. Time, climatic stability and productivity act together. A hot desert can be species-poor.  ·  Endemic means the species is found nowhere else, not merely that it is rare inside Nepal. A widespread species that is uncommon in one valley is not an endemic.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Plot the idea of log S against log A and mark z as the slope.  ·  List the two hotspot tests and apply them to a made-up region.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Equator = more species. Poles = fewer. Remember time + stability + energy.  ·  Hotspot = many unique plants AND most of the habitat already gone. Both tests are required.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Why does a log-log plot of species against area become a straight line?  ·  Explain why z is larger for islands and continents than for small sample plots.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Draw or describe the species-area curve and write both the power form and the log form.  ·  Name Nepal's two hotspots and the two criteria, with the numbers 1,500 and 70 percent.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Latitudinal diversity gradient  ·  Species-area relationship  ·  Slope z  ·  Biodiversity hotspot criteria

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Latitudinal gradient: species richness generally increases toward the equator.  ·  Species-area law: S = c A^z, and log S = log c + z log A.  ·  z is shallow (about 0.1-0.2) for local samples and steeper for continents and islands.  ·  Nepal lies in two hotspots, the Himalaya and Indo-Burma.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: There are 36 recognised global biodiversity hotspots. Two of them, Himalaya and Indo-Burma, include parts of Nepal.  ·  More than half of the world's species live in tropical regions, which cover a much smaller share of the land surface.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: A region has 2,000 endemic plants but has lost only 20 percent of its forest. Is it a hotspot? Say why.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: A 10-fold increase in area does not give a 10-fold increase in species, because z is well below 1.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: Species richness of most groups generally increases toward the → B  ·  The species-area relationship is written as → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: Species richness is not spread evenly. The strongest global pattern is the latitudinal gradient: the number of species of most groups rises from the poles toward the equator, so tropical forests and coral reefs hold far more species than tundra or boreal forest.  ·  Two ideas explain that gradient. The tropics have had a longer uninterrupted time for speciation, and a more stable climate, so extinction rates stay lower. Higher solar energy also supports higher productivity and, through that, more niches.  ·  The species-area relationship says that larger areas hold more species. Plotted as species against area it is a rectangular hyperbola, S = c A^z. On a log-log graph it becomes a straight line, log S = log c + z log A.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Nepal's altitude gradient  ·  Hotspot rule: at least 1,500 endemic vascular plants and over 70 percent habitat loss.  ·  Pair each pattern with a Nepal example: latitude (Terai versus alpine), area (larger continuous forest versus a fragment), hotspot (Himalaya, Indo-Burma).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: The log form is the one used to read z as the slope of a straight line.  ·  Alexander von Humboldt described the species-area relationship: within a region, species richness increases with the area explored, but with a decreasing slope.  ·  Tropics hold more species because of greater evolutionary time, climatic stability and higher productivity.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Nepal's biodiversity is high for its area because of the sharp altitude range from the Terai to the high Himalaya.  ·  State the latitudinal gradient and give one reason it exists.  ·  Write the species-area equation and say what z means.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Name the two hotspots that include Nepal and the two numerical tests for a hotspot.  ·  The slope z is about 0.1 to 0.2 when the areas are samples inside one continent. It rises to about 0.6 to 1.2 for whole continents or islands, because isolation adds species that occur nowhere else.  ·  Nepal is small in area but sits where two global biodiversity hotspots meet: the Himalaya and the Indo-Burma region. A hotspot must have at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species and must have lost more than 70 percent of its original habitat.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Inside Nepal, richness is highest in the mid-hills and the tropical lowland forests, while many endemics are concentrated in the high mountains. Altitude, rainfall and the east-west moisture gradient all change which species can live there.  ·  # Patterns of biodiversity — global and Nepal ## 1.
